title: The Band Plan — Where You're Allowed to Operate
subtitle: A built-in, plain-language reference to the U.S. amateur band plan (FCC Part 97) so you can confirm a frequency is legal for your license and mode before you transmit — right beside your recommendations.
in_this_chapter: What the band plan is and why it's in the program
Reading a band: sub-bands by license class and mode
How it works with your recommendations and calling frequencies
An important note on staying legal and current

callout.label: QUICK VERSION
callout.text: The **Band Plan** tab is a quick reference to which frequencies you're allowed to use, broken down by license class (Technician, General, Amateur Extra) and mode (voice, Morse code, digital). Before you transmit on a frequency the planner suggested, glance here to confirm it's inside your privileges. It covers the U.S. HF bands through 70 centimeters.

blocks.h1: What This Is / What It Is For

blocks.p: In the United States, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) — the government agency that regulates radio — sets rules (called **Part 97**) for exactly which frequencies each class of amateur license may use, and for which modes. Operating outside your privileges is against the rules. The **Band Plan** tab puts those rules right in the program, in plain language, so you can check a frequency without digging out a chart. It's a reference, not something you configure.

callout.label: JARGON, IN PLAIN WORDS
callout.text: **Band plan:** the agreed-and-regulated map of a band — which slices are for voice, which for Morse code (CW), which for digital modes, and which license classes may use each slice. **Part 97:** the section of U.S. federal rules that governs amateur radio.

blocks.p: Click **Band Plan** in the navigation bar. You'll see the amateur bands laid out from the lowest frequency (160 meters) up through the higher HF bands and into VHF/UHF (up to 70 centimeters), each with its sub-bands.
Each band is broken into **sub-bands** — segments set aside for particular modes and license classes. For each segment you'll see, in plain terms:

rows: The start and end of the segment, in megahertz (MHz).
What you may transmit there — for example CW (Morse code), phone (voice, such as SSB), or digital/data.
Which license classes may use that segment (Technician, General, or Amateur Extra).

blocks.p: So, for example, you can quickly confirm whether a voice frequency on 40 meters is open to a General-class operator, or whether a stretch of 20 meters is CW-only. The data reflects the current U.S. rules, including recent changes.
U.S. amateur licenses come in three active classes, each with more privileges than the last:

bullets: **Technician** — the entry-level license. Full privileges on VHF/UHF and limited HF privileges (notably some CW, and voice on part of 10 meters).
**General** — substantial HF privileges across most bands, enough for worldwide operating.
**Amateur Extra** — the top class, adding the exclusive bottom segments of several HF bands.

blocks.p: The tab shows which segments belong to which class so you can see, at a glance, what your license covers — and what upgrading would add.

blocks.h1: How It Works With Your Recommendations

blocks.p: The Band Plan tab pairs naturally with the planning screen. When the planner recommends a band and shows its **calling frequencies** (Chapter 4), pop over here to confirm those frequencies are within your license privileges and set for the mode you intend. The planner tells you *which band is best*; the band plan confirms *where on it you may legally operate*.

callout.label: YOU ARE RESPONSIBLE FOR OPERATING LEGALLY
callout.text: This tab is a helpful, good-faith reference built from the FCC Part 97 rules, but the **official FCC rules are the final authority.** Band plans can change, and this reference could lag a change. Always operate within your actual license privileges, and if in doubt, check the current official rules. The program never transmits for you — every transmission is your responsibility as the licensed operator.

rows: I'm not sure which class applies to me
Use the class you hold (Technician, General, or Amateur Extra). If you're unsure, check your FCC license record.
A calling frequency the planner showed isn't in my privileges
Then don't use that exact frequency — find a segment for your class and mode within the same band, or operate a mode your class allows there.
The band I want isn't shown
The tab covers the U.S. amateur bands from 160 meters through 70 centimeters. Bands outside that range aren't listed.
I think a segment is out of date
Treat the official FCC Part 97 rules as authoritative and operate accordingly; the tab is a convenience reference, not a legal document.
